findings.claim: The requirement says no new setting is needed and an opt-out is optional, but the change adds a new public API property GeneratedMessagePackResolverAttribute.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage and a new README-documented opt-out. This is permitted but expands the public API surface across four target frameworks. Whether the team wants that is not recorded.

receipt_plan.detail: Read GeneratedMessagePackResolverAttribute.cs:30-34 and the four PublicAPI.Unshipped.txt additions. The REQ-2297 acceptance criteria call an opt-out optional and give no maintainer decision.

findings.claim: The opt-out is read only from the [GeneratedMessagePackResolver] attribute. Formatters generated without a resolver attribute, such as the default resolver or assemblies with no attribute, fall back to the default of true and cannot be opted out. The opt-out is therefore not available everywhere generated code is emitted.

receipt_plan.detail: Generate formatters with no [GeneratedMessagePackResolver] attribute or with a different resolver config. Assert that no opt-out path exists and that the attribute is always emitted.

findings.claim: The CompositeResolver template emits the attribute unconditionally and ignores Options.Generator.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage. The other templates honor the opt-out, so with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage=false the composite resolver is still decorated. The README states that opting out removes the attribute, and the opt-out test asserts it is absent from every generated file, so the test may not exercise a composite resolver.

receipt_plan.detail: Set ExcludeFromCodeCoverage=false and generate a CompositeResolver (the tests do not cover one). Assert that the output does not contain the attribute.

findings.claim: The attribute is guarded with #if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK. ExcludeFromCodeCoverage exists on netstandard2.0 as of .NET Core 2.0 only in newer targets. The requirement says generated code must be decorated, but netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework consumers, who may be a large share of the user base, get no exclusion. The README does document the gap.

receipt_plan.detail: Read the guard in all templates and README.md:1640. It contradicts the acceptance criterion that all generated code is decorated, unless 'attribute must exist there or be conditionally emitted' is accepted.

findings.claim: Only top-level generated types and the nested FormatterCache helper types are decorated. Nesting partial types emitted by EmitNestingTypesAndNamespaces are user-declared partials and are left undecorated, which may be fine. The TransformUtilities change from '{' to '{\r\n' alters generated output for all nested generic-constrained types and is not related to this requirement.

receipt_plan.detail: Rerun the snapshot tests and inspect the diffs for nested types with constraints. Check that only the intended whitespace change appears.

questions.text: Should the opt-out setting exist at all, and should it be configurable beyond the resolver attribute?
options: Resolver attribute property only (the current approach)
An MSBuild property or analyzer config as well
questions.why_it_matters: The requirement allows either an unconditional attribute or an opt-out. If the answer is unconditional, the new public API and README text should be removed. If a wider setting is wanted, the current attribute-only scope is incomplete.

interpretations.label: A
interpretations.summary: Decorate all generated types, with the attribute emitted by default and an opt-out via a new GeneratedMessagePackResolver.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage property. Keep the #if guard for netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework.

interpretations.label: B
interpretations.summary: Decorate all generated types unconditionally with no setting. Remove the new attribute property, the PublicAPI entries, the Options.Generator.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage plumbing and the README opt-out text, and drop the conditionals in the templates.
